items._excerpt: Millar Western announced indefinite curtailment of Quesnel River Pulp. Millar Western Forest Products Ltd. will indefinitely curtail operations at its Quesnel River Pulp mill, citing market conditions and uncertainty surrounding economic fibre supply. The *Quesnel Cariboo Observer* obtained a copy of a letter sent out on Nov. 9, to employees at the Quesnel River Pulp mill. In the letter, executive chair and CEO Karl Meyers said the company had made the “very difficult decision” to curtail Quesnel River Pulp mill for an indefinite period. “Based on current contractual obligations, we will continue operating the effluent system for twelve months, or until we can reach an acceptable alternative,” Meyers said in the letter. “We will continue to complete an orderly shutdown of the balance of the operations over the next several weeks, setting it up for a potential restart in the future.” In August, Millar Western announced temporary curtailment of operations until at least November. Meyers said the company reviewed all alternatives before concluding that an indefinite curtailment was the only viable option at this time. According to the letter, the duration of the curtailment remains unknown and will depend on market conditions and the availability of economic fibre supply. “As a result, we will be terminating employment for all those impacted and providing severance compensation and other support,” Meyers wrote. He added the company will also provide continuation of certain benefits and access to employee and family assistance resources, with details to be outlined in individual severance letters. Meyers said Millar Western will also look at filling vacancies at other company operations with displaced employees. “For those who will continue to work, the period between now and your final day of employment will be considered as working notice,” he said. According to the letter, to qualify for severance, employees must remain active until their last scheduled day of work.

From spectators gathering for a flag-raising at a new Cenotaph in 1968 to veterans marching to city hall for a Korean War plaque dedication in 1994, Williams Lake has a long tradition of honouring those who served – one that continues. The Williams Lake and District Cenotaph was built in 1968 below the former War Memorial Hospital, a joint undertaking by the municipality and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 to honour the area’s war dead, according to the Veterans Affairs Canada’s website. The Cariboo War Memorial Hospital opened in May 1925, partly funded by the community of Soda Creek to honour fallen First World War soldiers. In 1968, the _Williams Lake Tribune_ reported on spectators gathering for a flag-raising ceremony at the new monument. Sixteen years later, the cenotaph was moved beside city hall and rededicated on Nov. 3, 1984, in conjunction with the dedication of the new municipal building. Days after the cenotaph’s rededication beside city hall, the _Tribune’s_ Nov. 8, 1984 edition outlined the plans for that year’s Remembrance Day Observance, bringing together veterans, students and community groups. The service began at 10:45 a.m. at the Elks Hall on Nov. 11, 1984 with the Williams Lake Community Band playing O Canada and a student from Anne Stevenson Junior Secondary School’s drama class reading In Flanders Field. Bill Lannigan and A.E McMath read the names of the former residents who died in the First and Second World Wars, followed by the Last Post and two minutes of silence. items.title: [thestar.com] Supreme Court hears challenge to Canada’s ban on 2,500 firearm types
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The Supreme Court of Canada began hearing a challenge Monday to the federal ban on more than 2,500 types of firearms the government classifies as assault-style weapons. The appeal follows two lower-court defeats for gun owners, advocacy groups and businesses challenging cabinet’s authority to prohibit the guns through regulations. The ban includes some firearms used for hunting and sport shooting. The government prohibited 1,500 models and variants, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14, in May 2020 and later expanded the list. Federal lawyers argue cabinet acted reasonably to address public-safety risks, while appellants say the regulations exceeded the authority Parliament granted and failed to account for lawful sporting and hunting uses. The hearings continue Tuesday, and a decision is expected by the end of 2027 at the latest. The possession amnesty runs until 90 days after the court rules.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, ends Banff rescue-dog program
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Parks Canada expects to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments and discontinue its Banff search-and-rescue dog program as part of $145 million in cuts over three years. The agency sent workforce-adjustment notices to 2,917 employees and says it will make individual decisions in the coming weeks. The Canadian Avalanche Rescue Dog Association and British Columbia Search Dog Association have urged the agency to reverse the cancellation, warning it could weaken rescue capacity. Parks Canada says it will shift wardens to a regional model focused on high-risk areas and that wardens can enforce park law without dogs. The associations say they are working on a short-term volunteer response during avalanche season.

When Paracel arrived in Tacuarita, an Indigenous community of homes made from planks and plastic sheeting in Paraguay’s poorest region, six years ago, it was a welcome sight. The company improved the dirt roads and dug an electric-powered well, saving villagers a two-mile journey to fetch water from a cattle pond that often made them sick. It also gave dozens of local people forestry jobs.

“They fulfilled all their promises,” says Florencio Garcete, 55, chief of the Mbya Guaraní community of 211 people.

🏔️ ✏️

The U.S. Department of Agriculture is moving forward with nearly $4 million in grants to 10 Kansas meat processors to expand capacity and give livestock producers more local processing options. The funding is part of a $57.4 million round covering 147 awards in 40 states through the Meat and Poultry Processing Expansion Program. USDA said it can begin obligating the grants after completing the congressional notification period. The largest Kansas grant, $2 million for Plainview Beef Company in Peabody, will help renovate and equip a processing facility, including cold storage, packaging, rendering and wastewater systems. USDA says the projects aim to expand market access for independent producers and increase competition among processors. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said, “A strong, independent processing sector is essential to our food security, and these Kansas processors build the resilient supply chain this country needs”.

items.title: [globalnews.ca] Carney sets six December byelections, giving Liberals chance to widen majority
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called federal byelections for Dec. 7 in six ridings across Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan: Scarborough North and Brantford—Brant South in Ontario, and Yorkton—Melville in Saskatchewan. The three Quebec contests are Laurier—Sainte-Marie, Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie and Saint-Hyacinthe—Bagot—Acton. The races will fill vacancies left by MPs from several parties. The Liberals hold 173 of the House of Commons’ 343 seats. Winning any of the vacant ridings would increase that total, although losing all six would not cost them the ability to govern. In Brantford—Brant South, Conservative nominee and Brantford Mayor Kevin Davis faces Liberal Joy O’Donnell and independent candidate Dave Carroll, who had sought the Conservative nomination. Advance voting is scheduled for Nov. 27-30, with special ballots available before Dec. 1.

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

Holger Peters, a farmer in Schleswig-Holstein, plans to replace grain production on his 340 hectares of arable land with perennial silphium over the next two years. He has planted 125 hectares so far. He says grain production has become barely profitable, while silphium can supply his biogas plant and may also provide a peat substitute for horticultural growing media. Polish cabbage and potato growers are also reporting weak returns: cabbage for processing is selling at about 50 groszy per kilogram, while wholesale potato prices in Łódź ranged from 53 groszy to 1.07 zlotys per kilogram on Oct. 30. Potato farmers have sought higher fuel-tax refunds, but the agriculture ministry has instead pointed to promotional campaigns with retailers.

Katie Hobbs declared a statewide emergency Monday to help local authorities clear roads, repair infrastructure and assist displaced residents. Flooding damaged roads and bridges, stranded residents and caused sewage to back up into some homes. Although rain had ended in parts of the Southwest by Monday, flooding along some swollen waterways could continue through at least Tuesday.

items.title: [Fast Company] DOJ sues Lyft for allegedly denying rides to people with disabilities
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit against Lyft, accusing the company of discriminating against passengers with disabilities who seek rides on its platform.

The federal lawsuit, filed Monday, says Lyft “is aware of, but fails to prevent and remedy” several discriminatory practices against riders who need accommodations under the Americans With Disabilities Act. That includes denying rides to people who have service animals or use stowable wheelchairs and refusing to let passengers with mobility issues sit in the front seat, the suit alleges.

“Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on ride-share services free of discrimination,” said Jesus A. Osete, acting assistant attorney general, in a statement. “We intend to uphold the ADA’s promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services.”

Lyft firmly rejected the accusations in a statement.

The lawsuit is the latest from the federal government that targets ride-hailing companies for the treatment of would-be riders with disabilities. The administration filed a similar lawsuit against Uber last year, which is ongoing. Uber settled a separate suit in 2022, and Lyft settled a different one in 2020. The companies stress that their policies and in-app tools require that drivers provide ADA accommodations and remind them of the consequences of refusing to do so.

The new lawsuit against Lyft named several examples of people across the country who hailed a ride on the platform but had one—or, in some cases, several—drivers refuse to take them to their destination, including as recently as last month. Those individuals experienced delays in getting to medical appointments, cancellation fees, and other issues as a result, the suit said.

Lyft policies require drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or mobility devices, and “drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation,” the company said in a statement.

“We’ve cooperated with the DOJ throughout its review and remain committed to serving every rider, including riders with disabilities,” the company said.

The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The Department of Justice said it is seeking $53 million for individuals who have been discriminated against and have submitted complaints to Lyft or the department.

—By Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press

items.title: [efeagro.com] Hackers raise supermarket freezer temperatures across Europe, spoiling food
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Cyberattacks disrupted refrigeration at grocery stores and other businesses in several European countries overnight into Nov. 2, raising temperatures in some units to 50°C and prompting businesses to discard food or remove it as a precaution. Affected countries included Belgium, Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia, Finland and Luxembourg; reports also described incidents in Italy, though the extent there remains unclear. In Belgium, Delhaize reported refrigeration problems in about 40 stores, Carrefour in 15 and Spar in five. Ireland’s SuperValu reported incidents at 13 stores, while refrigeration supplier Danfoss said at least 17 Dutch businesses were affected. The attackers appear to have remotely changed settings on connected equipment, in some cases activating defrost mode. European Agriculture and Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen described the repeated attacks as an attempt to disrupt food supply and weaken consumer trust, but said food security was not currently threatened. Belgian federal prosecutors opened an investigation, but no group has claimed responsibility and authorities have not established whether the incidents were part of one operation. Italy scheduled a government crisis meeting for Nov. 3 with national cybersecurity and intelligence officials.

items.title: [theconversation.com] Study finds prosecutions of African ruling families do not necessarily change institutions
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A study of six African countries finds that prosecuting former leaders’ relatives can punish individuals or shift power among elites without changing the institutions that enabled abuses. Researcher Michael Asiedu examined Angola, Gabon, Senegal, Egypt, Tunisia and The Gambia, tracing court cases, official inquiries and asset measures. The study finds that outcomes depend partly on whether successors weaken a family’s political protection and whether defendants are within reach of domestic courts. Tunisia held competitive elections and adopted a new constitution after prosecutions in 2011, but President Kais Saied began concentrating executive power in 2021. In Angola, the former ruling party stayed in power after a former president’s son was prosecuted.

items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Earth’s energy imbalance has reached its highest level since monitoring began, and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Global surface temperature averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level from January through September; a developing, unusually strong El Niño could push the annual figure higher and prolong extreme heat into 2027. The agency released its report as the U.N. climate summit COP31 opened in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiations scheduled through Nov. 20. The agency says each of the past 12 years ranked among the 12 warmest on record, with 2023-2026 likely to be the four warmest years. Greenhouse gases from human activity are trapping heat; the ocean absorbs about 90% of the excess, while sea levels and ocean temperatures have reached records. The WMO warns that the accumulating heat will intensify heat waves, droughts, tropical cyclones and heavy rain. A separate U.N. Environment Programme assessment says warming will exceed 1.5°C under every plausible emissions pathway. Returning below that threshold this century would require near-zero emissions and the removal of hundreds of billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide. The WMO’s full 2026 climate report is due in March 2027.

items.content_html:

El Niño-related peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia are projected to push land-use carbon emissions higher in 2026, bringing total global CO₂ emissions to 43.3 billion tonnes even as fossil-fuel emissions edge down, according to the Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment. The researchers link the rise in land-use emissions to drier conditions and fires often ignited by human activity. The 21st Global Carbon Budget, published Nov. 10 in Earth System Science Data and presented during the U.N. climate conference in Antalya, projects 5.1 billion tonnes of emissions from land-use change this year. The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. Separately, an analysis of Chinese data found that emissions fell 3.1% in July-September, the country’s steepest quarterly drop since pandemic lockdowns in 2022.

items.title: [space.com] Soviet Union sent Laika into orbit aboard Sputnik 2 with no return plan
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 2 with Laika aboard on Nov. 3, 1957, making the Moscow stray the first animal to orbit Earth. The spacecraft had no system to bring her back, and Laika died within hours as the capsule overheated, according to later accounts. The flight came less than a month after Sputnik 1 and aimed to test how a living organism responded to launch and weightlessness. Sensors transmitted Laika’s vital signs to Earth, but Soviet officials initially said she had survived for days. Details of her early death from overheating became public decades later. Sputnik 2 remained in orbit until it burned up on re-entry on April 14, 1958.

The spacecraft had no system to bring her back, and Laika died within hours as the capsule overheated, according to later accounts (space.com, astronomy.com, mondo.ba). The flight came less than a month after Sputnik 1 and aimed to test how a living organism responded to launch and weightlessness. Flight response: During the ride to orbit, Laika’s heart rate reached 260 beats per minute, about three times normal, and her breathing increased four to five times above usual (reddit.com). Cabin design: The dog cabin measured about 0.8 metres long and 0.64 metres in diameter and included a small window and television camera (reddit.com). Ethical legacy: Laika’s mission helped draw public attention to the ethics of animal experiments in space exploration (yam.com). Earlier animal tests: Before Laika’s orbital flight, the United States had sent fruit flies on a suborbital flight, while the Soviet Union had conducted suborbital dog tests (yam.com).
